TWO waits in an end-to-end spec, each buying a strictly later clock second after a password change so the token minted next is accepted: the `iat` vs `passwordChangedAt` comparison in middleware/auth.ts ceils a millisecond timestamp to the next second while a JWT `iat` has one-second precision, so a token minted in the same second is legitimately rejected. Both are load-bearing, measured: removing the first turned 'revoke refresh tokens after password change' red in 2 of 3 repeats, and removing the second turned 'preserve vault items after password change' red in 1 of 4. A THIRD occurrence was removed in Phase 19 rather than ledgered: 'change password and authenticate with new password' ends at the login response and never presents the token it mints, so the comparison never runs there - 3 of 3 repeats green without it. REMOVAL CONDITION CORRECTED IN PHASE 19. This entry used to name the injectable clock as its removal condition, alongside SUP-0021 to SUP-0024. That was wrong, and those four are now gone precisely because the clock DID reach them: they are vitest tests whose server runs in the same worker, so freezing Date there is seen by the code under test. These two are not. They are Playwright specs driving APIRequestContext, and the clock that must advance belongs to the API server in a SEPARATE PROCESS; no vitest fake reaches it, and page.clock fakes only the browser. The alternatives are worse than the debt: flooring passwordChangedAt to the second would open a one-second window in which a token issued before a password change is still accepted, which is a security regression, and a test phase may not change production behaviour. These are real waits on a real production property rather than concealed flakiness. Removed by an injectable clock the SERVER can be started with, or by an end-to-end harness able to advance the server's clock; neither exists today.

The E2E suite shares one dev server and one in-memory MongoDB across specs, so a second worker would race on both. It is a real constraint rather than a hidden flake, but it IS single-worker execution and the doctrine says to write that down. Phase 19 measures the flake rate and owns removing it; the short expiry is deliberate.

Moving the activator to be a child of the card left the label a sibling of it, so the label's onClick={(e) => e.stopPropagation()} now stops propagation to nothing and was deleted. That arrow function is the one instrumentable line. The coverage scope is unchanged (packages/client/vitest.config.ts untouched), the measured file set is unchanged at 120 files, and no coverage percentage moved: line 98.69, branch 92.45, function 97.95 before and after. Keeping the handler purely to hold the denominator at 7038 would be dead code retained to satisfy a metric, which is the move this ledger exists to make visible.

test:resource's time and memory budgets can see a STEP CHANGE and nothing smaller, and this records how much smaller. Measured over five consecutive runs of the whole suite on an idle reference machine, the good runs themselves vary by 11-50 percent: rotation-volume rssGrowthMb spans 66.68-126.05 MB (50 percent of its median), backup-streaming durationMs spans 268-443 ms (49.7 percent), backup-full-vault durationMs 439-724 ms (47.1 percent). Every ceiling is therefore set at 1.6x-11x the observed maximum, which means a real regression smaller than roughly 1.7x on memory or 3x on time passes unseen. Shipping tighter numbers would produce a gate that fires on a loaded laptop, and a gate that fires for reasons unrelated to the code is a gate that gets deleted. ONE budget is exempt from this gap and is the reason the streaming scenario has a real verdict: backup-streaming rssGrowthMb, whose good band (43.43-58.11 MB over eleven runs) and regression band (118.54-156.41 MB over three runs of the find().lean() rewrite) do not overlap, so the 95 MB ceiling sits clear of both; and backup-streaming documentsDelivered, which measured 3320 of 10000 in eleven out of eleven runs against 10003 for the regression, with no spread at all. The gap is closed either by a metric with no noise band (a counter read from the server, as documentsDelivered is) or by a dedicated benchmark harness that controls for machine load; adding either is worth more than tightening these numbers.

entries.symbol: emailSchema's .trim() and its 'must have a TLD' refine
entries.reason: Twenty mutants in lines 1-27 of auth.ts are BEHAVIOURALLY EQUIVALENT rather than unasserted, and the reason is that the code they mutate is unreachable as a decider. emailSchema is z.email().max(254).toLowerCase().trim().refine(hasTld). The refine's own comment says zod accepts user@host, and that was true of the zod version it was written against; the installed zod 4 rejects it in z.email() itself, along with every other input the refine rejects. Its regex is anchored, admits no whitespace, forbids consecutive dots, requires each host label to start alphanumeric and requires a 2-or-more-letter TLD, so host.length === 0, host.startsWith('.'), host.endsWith('.'), labels.length < 2, an empty label and a label containing whitespace or an at sign are all already impossible by the time the refine runs. The same argument covers .trim(): a value with leading or trailing whitespace never reaches it. Verified structurally AND empirically - 1,248 addresses built from 6 local parts x 13 hosts x 4 leading x 4 trailing padding characters, comparing z.email().max(254).toLowerCase() against the full schema, produced ZERO disagreements in acceptance or in output. The code is KEPT rather than deleted, as defense-in-depth against a future loosening of zod's email format, on the same footing as toolsController's assertImportFieldLengths (which CLAUDE.md records as deliberately uncovered for the same reason). Removal condition: this entry goes away if zod's email check is ever replaced or loosened, at which point the refine becomes reachable and every one of these mutants becomes a missing assertion. What IS asserted, in tests/schema-bounds.test.ts, is the one transform that does change a value that reaches it: .toLowerCase(), which matters because the email is the PBKDF2 salt.

entries.symbol: formatBytes guards, normalizeUri optional-s, and the noUncheckedIndexedAccess fallbacks
entries.reason: Seven survivors in utils/index.ts are behaviourally equivalent, verified by REIMPLEMENTING each mutant beside the original and comparing outputs rather than by reading the code. (1) formatBytes line 12, 'bytes < 0' becoming 'bytes <= 0': zero is returned as '0 B' by the very next line either way. (2) formatBytes line 13, the 'bytes === 0' early return deleted: Math.log(0) is -Infinity, which the Math.max(...,0) clamp on line 21 turns into exponent 0, so the function still returns '0 B'. Both compared over 334 values - every power of two from 2^-40 to 2^63 and its neighbours, plus 0, -0, negatives, Infinity, NaN, Number.MIN_VALUE, Number.EPSILON and each unit boundary - with ZERO disagreements. The early return is kept because it states the intent at the top rather than leaving it to a clamp four lines down. (3) normalizeUri line 32, '/^(https?:|mailto:)/i' becoming '/^(https:|mailto:)/i': an http: URI that stops matching the first guard is caught by the SECOND guard on line 34 ('some other scheme, leave it alone') and returned unchanged, so the two are indistinguishable from outside; compared over 15 scheme shapes with zero disagreements. What is NOT equivalent, and is now asserted in tests/utils.test.ts, is either ANCHOR being dropped from either pattern. (4) Three NoCoverage mutants on the '?? ' and "?? 'B'" fallbacks at lines 6, 7 and 22: these exist to satisfy noUncheckedIndexedAccess and are unreachable - local[0] and local[local.length-1] are defined whenever atIndex > 0, and sizes[i] is defined because i is clamped to the array's own length. CLAUDE.md already records this class as deliberately uncovered ('noUncheckedIndexedAccess nullish guards'), and lighting them up would need a contrived mock of an index operation. Removal condition: (1)-(3) go away if the guards they duplicate are removed; (4) goes away if the compiler stops requiring the fallback.
